newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi real GDP growth in 1997 seen at 2.0 percent.
newsitem.headline: Saudi real GDP growth in 1997 seen at 2.0 percent.

text.p: Saudi Arabia's real gross domestic product growth in 1997 will be two percent, well below last year's rate when high oil prices pushed real GDP up five percent, a leading Saudi-based economist said.
But the kingdom still needs to address economic challenges ranging from government overspending to unemployment, Henry Azzam, chief economist at the National Commercial Bank, said.

In a study obtained by Reuters on Wednesday, Azzam said high oil prices in 1996 did not only boost government revenues and return the current account to surplus "but also alleviated the need for the government to adopt stricter austerity measures".
He forecast nominal GDP growth of three percent in 1997, compared to 8.6 percent in 1996. Inflation is seen at one percent this year, from 0.9 percent last year.

Higher oil prices in 1996 pushed Saudi's revenues some $12 billion over projections and enabled it to catch up on most of its arrears payments. Its 1997 budget projected a deficit of $4.5 billion -- steady at the actual 1996 deficit but below the $4.9 billion spending-revenue gap forecast in January 1996.

Azzam said the successive decline in deficits over the past few years showed that the world's largest oil producer and exporter, "is on target to attain a balanced budget by the year 2000" -- one of the targets of the 1995-2000 development plan.

He said Saudi Arabia has taken steps "to strengthen the structure of the economy, particularly in the areas of fiscal and financial sector reforms" and was now "in a solid position to confront its remaining economic and financial challenges".
"There is a general recognition in the kingdom today that structural imbalances are unlikely to be eliminated by a sudden surge in oil prices.

"Even if oil prices maintain the high level attained in 1996, this would not solve any of the fundamental challenges that the country faces, be it overspending, increasing private sector participation, boosting productivity of public sector institutions, upgrading the legal and financial infrastructure, reducing unemployment and downsizing the public sector.

"It is hoped that the recent rise in oil prices would not lead to the postponement of the reform policies that were introduced in the past two years in order not to lose the momentum for change that is already visible," Azzam said.

He expected a trade surplus of $26.8 billion this year after an estimated $29.3 billion in 1996. After returning to surplus for the first time in 13 years in 1996, at $187 million, the current account is expected to show a $3.2 billion deficit.
Azzam projected a balance of payments surplus of $1.4 billion from $1.5 billion last year.
